ABSTRACT 
 
 
 It is vital to discover the shelf life of the leafy vegetables in order to maintain the safety,quality 
of the nutritional content in addition to minimizing the wastage of the harvested products. Leafy 
vegetables such as Spinach hold great value among consumers.They can consistently provide 
leafy vegetables over the whole harvesting period. On the other hand, the leafy vegetables such 
as Palak have high demand in the market and high price as well. They are perishable goods that 
could easily spoil before they reach their end-users because of factors such as wilting, yellowing, 
physical damages, and the growth of microorganisms. The traditional techniques have been 
applied to perform the quality control tasks in the case of perishable commodities.  
 
However, the techniques require human intervention in the form of visual examination 
in addition to professional expertise for performing lab tests on them which were long 
procedures. 
We will design an AI algorithm to predict the shelf life of the harvest using the images of the 
products to estimate their freshness and remaining shelf life. Our code for developing our AI 
will involve visual characteristics such as color, texture, structure of the leafy green vegetable to 
categorize the image file based on its freshness level. In turn, our product will be categorized 
into one of the three levels namely Fresh, Midlife, and Near Spoilage depending on the freshness 
level detected from our AI code. This way, we will be able to detect the shelf life of our product 
in terms of days. 
 
    Keywords: 
    Artificial Intelligence, Shelf Life Prediction, Leafy Vegetables, Image Processing, Convolutional 
Neural Network, MobileNetV2, Freshness Classification

1. INTRODUCTION 
 
 
       1.1Motivation 
The use of leafy vegetables is vital because it guarantees the provision of nutrients, vitamins, and 
minerals to our bodies. However, spinach and other leafy vegetables fall under the category of 
perishable foods owing to their high water content and delicate nature. After the harvesting 
process, leafy vegetables wilt, lose color, undergo structural changes, and become prone to 
bacterial infections. As a result, there are issues related to storage, transportation, and marketing 
of leafy vegetables. 
Presently, the assessment of the quality of leafy vegetables is conducted using visual 
inspection. The approach is subjective and imprecise. Although laboratory testing produces 
accurate results, it takes a substantial amount of time to execute. Hence, laboratory testing is 
impractical because it takes much time to conduct an analysis. The delay can cause food waste 
due to the early disposal of leafy vegetables or consumption of products that are of poor quality. 
Hence, food waste is not only a hindrance to economic efficiency but also results in unnecessary 
food losses. 
However, the development of Artificial Intelligence and image processing technologies 
has enabled the construction of an algorithm that will conduct non-destructive testing of the 
quality of leafy vegetables and provide estimations regarding the days left before expiration.This 
is why building an website is the goal of this project. 
 
1.2 Existing Systems 
Existing Systems For the problem of shelf life estimation of leafy vegetables, existing methods 
Tend to rely heavily on traditional approaches. Manual inspection is among the oldest methods 
that assess the freshness of the vegetables visually by looking at their appearance characteristics, 
such as their color, texture, firmness, wilting, etc.his approach, however, is very subjective and 
depends heavily on the person doingthe evaluation. It is also hard to scale since the process cannot be 
applied to mass-produced batches. The lab analysis of the product is another way of evaluating the 
freshness of vegetables, through microbial and chemical decomposition studies. 
While this method offers an accurate estimate of the product's quality, it is both costly 
slow, taking days or even weeks to return results.Temperatures and humidity levels can be used 
to estimate the product's shelf life. Another conventional approach would be using conventional

computer vision and machine learning to estimate the product's shelf life. This approach uses 
hand-coded features, such as color thresholding and texture extraction. 
  
Such an approach is often less accurate compared to the deep learning approach and 
requires additional procedures to ensure its effectiveness. Thus, the systems used currently are 
either expensive, subjective, indirect, or not very accurate in general. 
Therefore, there is a need to develop an automated, cheap, and AI-based approach to 
solving the problem. 
 
1.3 Literature Survey 
 
1.⁠ ⁠Predictive Microbiology-Based Shelf Life Prediction Modelling 
Author(s): Scott et al. Date: 1993 
Approach: Uses the predictive microbiology approach combined with the modelling technique 
based on square root and Arrhenius methods.In this context, analysis is carried out in order to

Key Contributions: Laid the groundwork for developing shelf-life predictions through 
temperature kinetic models which served as a base for further studies in food preservation.

Author(s): Zhang et al. Date: 2011

extreme conditions of stress. 
Key Contributions: The use of ASLT successfully helped to shorten the testing time without 
affecting prediction accuracy.  
3.⁠ ⁠Hybrid Kinetics – Machine Learning Model Approach

1.4 Challenges to existing system 
 
 The following difficulties are encountered in shelf-life prediction of leafy vegetables using the 
current technique. Firstly, there is an issue related to manual inspection. Manual inspection is 
performed by many people. Inspection is very subjective and relies on perception. It is important

4 
 
to realize that differences in perception can be significant,so manual inspection is rather 
subjective. What is more, the technique in question cannot be implemented for a large number 
of items because it takes much time. Thus,it works well when only a few items are inspected. 
Chemical and laboratory testing can be considered a fairly reliable method. However, it is rather 
expensive and requires much time. Chemical testing requires specific equipment as well as 
qualified personnel, so this method does not work well in farms and retail stores. The analysis 
of humidity and temperature provides just indirect information about the freshness of vegetables, 
while physical and visual characteristics are not checked. In addition,special equipment is 
required  
 
 
Traditional computer vision methods imply that the features have to be Selected manually 
(e.g., color and texture analysis). The problem with such approaches is related to their inability 
to operate under changing lighting conditions. Hence a new system is to be designed to overcome 
these problems. 
 
1.5 Proposed system 
 
 The proposed system is a shelf life prediction system that is driven by artificial intelligence and 
is used to predict the shelf life of leafy vegetables depending on the level of freshness using 
image analysis. Images of leafy vegetables, including spinach, mint, coriander, and cabbage, are 
taken using an RGB camera to be classified in accordance with the level of freshness. 
  
The pre-processing steps include resizing, normalizing, and augmenting of data to increase 
quality of inputs. The classification process utilizes Deep Learning and Transfer Learning 
algorithms together with MobileNetV2 network to identify critical features, such as color 
degradation and texture of leafy vegetables. The images are categorized as Fresh, Mild (mid-
life), and Rotten (near spoilage). Days of storage can be calculated for each category. The 
proposed system enables fast non-destructive testing of the freshness stage of the product 
without requiring any lab analysis or sensors. 
 
1.6 Objectives 
 
The critical elements that make up this study include: 
• ⁠Creation of novel deep learning approach to estimate the shelf-life of leafy vegetables by 
analyzing their images 
• Implementation of a CNN architecture that utilizes the MobileNetV2 framework to 
predictwhether the leafy vegetables belong to any of the three categories: fresh, mid-life, or

rotten. 
• Pre-processing of the input images through a number of image transformations such as 
scaling,normalization, and data augmentation. 
• Analysis of visual cues via imaging technologies in RGB format that detect the presence of 
certain characteristics in leafy vegetables including their color pattern, texture, or wilting state. 
• Estimation of the predicted shelf-life measured in days based on the results of freshness analysis. 
• Verification of the effectiveness of the design through leafy vegetable prototyping, i.e. spinach. 
 
 
  1.7 Methodology 
 
A number of structured steps are applied within the framework of the methodology for predicting 
the shelf life of newly developed system, including data gathering and Prediction. At first, images 
of leafy vegetables such as spinach, mint, coriander, cabbage are grouped into three clusters on 
the basis of their freshness (Fresh, Mild (Midlife), Rotten). At second, a procedure of train-test-
validation was implemented for more precise measurement of the model's performance. In terms 
of preprocessing, all images have been transformed in order to become equal in size to those of 
224 x 224 pixels, as required by the Base model. Apart from that, normalization of the pictures 
is also performed during this process for better results. 
 
  
 
Speaking about model creation, Transfer Learning is used through the implementation 
of pre-trained model – MobileNetV2. The Base model was frozen, while new layers were 
introduced to solve the task of classification (Global Average Pooling, Dropout (rate = 0.5), Dense 
layer, and Softmax activation). Optimization and validation of the model took place by using 
Adam optimizer and categorical cross-entropy loss function. Early stopping was used. Finally, 
class prediction and remaining shelf life calculation in days were made by the model.

1.9 Organization of the project 
 
The Shelf Life Prediction project consists of several stages that make up a development lifecycle 
from collecting raw data to the final testing. Initially, there is a stage associated with the collection 
of data. At this stage, images of the randomly selected leafy vegetables are collected and classified 
according to their level of freshness. After that, there is a stage called image preprocessing. Here, 
images are preprocessed, normalized, and augmented to have standardized inputs. 
  
  
Then follows the creation of a machine learning model using Transfer Learning algorithm 
and MobileNetV2 architecture. The created model classifies the level of freshness of an image by 
applying the technique of dropout regularization. After finishing the training process, the model 
is ready for prediction, which gives the number of days left for the shelf life. 
  
 
 Finally, there is a testing phase, during which the quality of the predictions will be

2. PROPOSED SYSTEM 
 
2.1 Architecture 
 
Architecture of the Proposed Shelf Life Prediction system.The Proposed Shelf-life Prediction 
system uses deep learning techniques by leveraging transfer learning from the MobileNetV2 
Convolutional Neural Network model. 
 
   Firstly, an image of leafy vegetables is captured and classified based on the condition of its 
freshness. Initially, an image of leafy vegetables having a dimension of 224x224x3 is obtained 
wherein the dimensions represent the RGB image of the leafy vegetables. Thereafter, the image 
is used as input data for the pre-trained MobileNetV2 Convolutional Neural Network.  
 
   The pre-trained base layers of the MobileNetV2 neural network are kept frozen in order to 
utilize the learned features such as edges, texture, colors, etc. Next comes the Global Average 
Pooling 2D layer in which high-dimensional feature maps are converted into 1-D vectors. 
Afterwards, a dropout layer with a probability of 0.5 is added.To avoid overfitting, the role of this 
layer is to drop out a few neurons randomly. After this, the output will be sent to a dense layer 
that has three neurons in it. Then, the Softmax activation function is employed to assign 
probabilities to each class. Finally, the output stage of classification will have three classes for 
freshness - fresh, mild, and rotten. Along with the classification outcome, the model provides the 
probability of the assigned class.

       2.2 Module level design 
 
The Shelf Life Prediction Application is made up of several modules that assist in predicting the 
freshness of the leafy vegetables as well as predicting their shelf life. 
 
2.1.1 Image input module 
Images are obtained through the use of the input image module. The input image module helps 
capture images using the camera or any other existing dataset. Once images have been obtained, 
there arises a need to resize the images to 224 x 224 x 3 for deep learning. 
 
2.1.2 Feature extraction module 
 
The input image is transformed into something meaningful through the use of the feature 
extraction module with the MobileNetV2 pre-trained model. The feature extraction module 
freezes the base layers of the input image to obtain features. 
2.1.3 Feature processing module 
The feature maps that are extracted from the image data are processed using a Global Average 
Pooling 2D layer. The purpose of this process is to convert the feature maps into a single 
dimensional feature vector. This approach simplifies the computation, ensuring only the 
important features are considered for classification. 
 
2.1.4 Regularization module 
A Dropout layer with a probability rate of 0.5 is used for preventing the issueof overfitting. In 
this module, some neurons are deactivated during training to make the model more generalizable. 
 
2.1.5 Classification module 
 
In the classification module, a Dense layer having three neurons with Softmax Activation 
Function is used to classify the image into one of the three stages of fruit freshness. 
 
2.1.6 Output module 
The output module outputs the result by showing the freshness category together with its 
confidence level. Using the category, the shelf life left for the leafy vegetable can be estimated.

3. IMPLEMENTATION AND TESTING 
 
3.1 Implementation 
The Shelf Life Prediction system is designed through a highly structured implementation strategy 
that entails the following stages; preparation, pre-processing, development, training and 
prediction models. The process of implementing this system involves employing Python 
Programming Language and deep neural networks. 
 
3.1.1 Dataset preparation 
 
A selection of some photos depicting common leafy vegetables such as spinach, mint, and  
coriander is included in this project. The different aged cabbages that have varying levels of 
decomposition are grouped into either fresh, mild or old. These photos are sorted out based on 
their categories by placing them in various folders for the generation of both the training and 
validation data sets. 
 
3.1.2 Data preprocessing 
 
All the images used in this project are adjusted to the size of 224 x 224 pixels to meet the input 
size of the classification model implemented. Implementation of MobileNetV2 network. Pixel 
Normalization is conducted within the range of 0 - 1. Two Data Augmentation strategies; image 
rotation and image flipping are applied. Image Rescaling and Image Zooming techniques are also 
applied during the training phase. 
 
3.1.3 Model development 
 
Transfer Learning was performed using the pre-trained model MobileNetV2.These models were 
trained with the use of data from ImageNet. The base layers of this model were freezed in order 
to preserve its trained features. Features. Additional layers were added such as Global Average 
Pooling to reduce the feature space dimension, Dropout (0.5) to prevent overfitting, and Dense 
layer. The output layer had three neurons with SoftMax activation for the classes “Fresh”, “Mild”, 
and “Rotten”.

3.1.4 Model training 
The training of the model was done by the Adam optimizer and categorical cross entropy loss. 
The entropy loss function was used during the training of the network models in different epochs. 
Accuracy on validation set. To prevent overfitting, the early stopping method was used. 
 
3.1.5 Prediction and Shelf Life estimation 
  After the training stage of the deep learning model has been done, the model gains the ability to 
predict the input data as being one among the three classes of data in the model. Prediction of the 
input data coordinates can be made by running the frame captured by the camera through the 
model. The class in consideration is the one used in this experiment. Prediction of the input images 
for each of the three classes was made depending on how accurate the model prediction would 
be. Based on the mapping stage, prediction of the class could estimate the days left for shelf life. 
 
3.2 Testing 
 
Test of the proposed prediction system would make the effectiveness of the system known. The 
next chapter will outline briefly the system of prediction that would be developed. To test the 
generalization ability of the dataset, images have been taken which belong to the test data set that 
has not been used previously. The testing of the model was conducted by providing test input 
images to the model and then those images were tested through our MobileNetV2 model that has 
been trained for this purpose.  
 
  
The method that has been employed to measure the quality of leafy vegetables through 
visual feature extraction has proven quite effective since a very high accuracy level was obtained. 
Spinach has been considered in our model. 
   
Furthermore, we have also tested shelf-life estimation module under room temperature. 
Unlike conventional approaches which rely on manual annotation techniques, predictions made

4. RESULTS AND DESCRIPTION 
 
 
The developed Shelf Life Prediction system incorporated the use of deep learning with the 
application of the MobileNetV2 model. The model utilized a dataset of images of leafy 
vegetables that were separated into three categories of class labels: Fresh,Mild (Mid-life), and 
Rotten. This was done using the Google Colab development environment that utilized all the 
necessary machine learning libraries. 
 
In the training process, the deep learning model learned how to analyze various visual 
features in relation to freshness. The learning process entailed the processes of image pre-
processing, feature extraction using MobileNetV2 model and finally image classification using 
the fully connected layer. 
 
The trained deep learning model could be able to predict the freshness stage of the leafy 
vegetable through the input images. Upon uploading a new image, the system evaluated its 
features and gave the output of freshness category with confidence score. From the results, it was 
evident that the deep learning model could effectively classify the freshness stages of the 
vegetable. 
 
The output of the system can therefore be regarded as an effective means of evaluating the 
freshness state of leafy vegetables. 
 
   
Therefore, it should be stated that thanks to this method of classifying products, it is 
now possible to estimate their freshness level and predict the amount of shelf life time left. Also, 
this system may potentially be improved by adding additional types of vegetables to classify their 
freshness.

5. CONCLUSION 
 
The Shelf-Life Prediction System utilizes a set of machine learning and image processing 
methods used for solving the issue of determining the freshness level of leafy greens. As for the 
key component of the system, it is the convolutional neural network. It is based on one particular 
type of neural network called MobileNetV2, which is specially developed for image recognition 
tasks. The process itself is rather simple and involves the analysis of the degree of the freshness 
factors present. In other words, there will be estimated the presence of Fresh, Mild, and Average 
degrees of freshness. 
 
  For detecting freshness level, it is critical to analyze a variety of visual attributes found in the 
vegetables. Such attributes may include changes in the color, which is an indicator of vegetable 
spoilage, texture changes that imply a loss of firmness and blurring or fading out that show 
deterioration. In addition, the system is also able to recognize patterns of vegetables' wilting, 
which include, for instance, vegetable leaves becoming soft and droopy, etc., which is one of the 
main attributes of a less fresh vegetable. Thus, through training on specific patterns, the CNN is 
able to accurately make forecasts upon receiving new images. 
 
The major advantage of such system lies in its ability to work fast and efficiently. As 
such, the system allows minimizing the use of human resources, avoiding human error and 
subjectivity and, therefore, working fast. In this respect, such a system would be particularly 
helpful when there is a necessity to inspect lots of vegetables, such as in markets or in 
warehouses. 
 
Moreover, such systems are also expected to become helpful when it comes to inspection 
of different food products other than vegetables. That is why, the presented approach may be 
considered useful for food quality control. With the help of early identification of food decay, 
the technology plays a huge role in food preservation, a problem that is very crucial globally.

Network Training 
Network training is a process used to adjust the weights of a neural network so that it can learn from data 
and make accurate predictions. It involves multiple steps, including weight initialization, activation 
calculations, clustering, and backpropagation. Below is a simplified and detailed explanation of the key

1. Introduction to Network Training 
When designing a neural network, one major challenge is ensuring it generalizes well to new data and 
does not overfit. Overfitting occurs when a network memorizes training data instead of learning 
meaningful patterns. To prevent this, various training techniques are used. 
One common method is the backpropagation algorithm, which adjusts network weights based on the 
error between predicted and actual values. Another approach is clustering hidden units to optimize 
network structure. 
2. Steps in Network Training 
A. Weight Initialization 
• 
Weights are the numerical parameters that determine how information flows through a network. 
• 
Proper initialization helps the network converge faster and prevents issues like vanishing 
gradients. 
• 
Weights can be initialized randomly or based on domain knowledge. 
B. Calculation of Activation 
• 
Each unit (or neuron) in the network computes an output based on its inputs and weights. 
• 
The activation function (e.g., sigmoid function) is used to determine the output of each neuron. 
                 
 
C. Clustering Hidden Units 
• 
Hidden units are grouped into clusters based on similarity. 
• 
The similarity is measured using weight vectors. 
• 
If the similarity is above a threshold (e.g., 0.85), the units are merged; otherwise, a new cluster is 
formed. 
• 
This step helps optimize the network and reduces redundancy. 
Clustering procedure: 
1. Start with no clusters.

2. Assign the first hidden unit to a new cluster. 
3. For each remaining hidden unit: 
o 
Find the most similar cluster. 
o 
If similarity > threshold, update weight vectors. 
o 
Otherwise, create a new cluster. 
After clustering, new hidden units are introduced with updated weight vectors. 
D. Weight Training using Backpropagation 
• 
Backpropagation is the most widely used training method. 
• 
It involves adjusting weights to minimize the difference between predicted and actual outputs. 
• 
This is done using gradient descent, which updates weights based on errors.

Network Revision and Issues in Knowledge-Based Neural Networks 
Network Revision 
Network revision in knowledge-based neural networks (KBNNs) involves refining and updating the 
network's structure and weights based on new data or insights. This process is crucial for maintaining the 
network's accuracy and relevance over time. The revision process typically includes the following steps: 
1. Mapping the Rule Base into a Neural Network: The initial domain knowledge, often in the 
form of rules, is mapped into a neural network architecture. This involves assigning input units to 
data attributes, output units to target concepts, and hidden units to intermediate concepts. 
2. Training the Neural Network: The network is trained using the backpropagation procedure on 
the training data. This step adjusts the weights of the connections to minimize the error between 
the network's output and the desired output. 
3. Revising the Trained Neural Network: After training, the network is revised to improve its 
performance. This involves detecting and correcting semantically incorrect connections, which 
are connections that do not align with the intended logic of the rules. 
4. Translating the Revised Neural Network into Rules: The revised network is translated back 
into a set of rules, which can be used to update the initial domain knowledge. 
Semantically Incorrect Connections: 
• 
Definition: Semantically incorrect connections are those where the weight (strength) of the 
connection does not align with the logical relationship between the nodes it connects. For 
example, a positive weight might indicate an excitatory connection, but if the actual relationship 
is inhibitory, the connection is semantically incorrect. 
• 
Detection: The consistent-shift algorithm is used to detect semantically incorrect connections. 
This algorithm compares the weights before and after training. If the weight shift is inconsistent 
(i.e., the weight moves in the opposite direction of what is expected), the connection is flagged as 
semantically incorrect. 
• 
Revision: Connections identified as semantically incorrect are either deleted or adjusted. Deletion 
of a connection from a conjunction unit to a disjunction unit means deleting a rule, while deletion 
of a connection from a disjunction unit or an input unit to a conjunction unit corresponds to 
generalizing a rule.

Issues in Network Revision 
Several issues arise during the network revision process, particularly in the context of knowledge-based 
neural networks: 
1. Strength of Initial Knowledge: 
o 
No Initial Knowledge: If there is no initial knowledge, the network must be built from 
scratch using a purely data-driven approach. This involves creating a fully connected 
multilayer neural network and training it on available data. 
o 
Strong Initial Knowledge: If the initial knowledge is strong, the network can be directly 
mapped from the existing rules without adding extra hidden units or connections. This 
simplifies the computation but requires that the initial knowledge is accurate and 
complete. 
o 
Weak or Incomplete Knowledge: If the initial knowledge is weak or incomplete, 
additional hidden units and connections must be added to the network. The number of 
hidden units required can be indicated by the error curve during training. Poor 
convergence suggests that more hidden units are needed. 
2. Preservation of Initial Semantics: 
o 
Semantics of Hidden Units: The semantics of a hidden unit are reflected by its input and 
output weight patterns. During training, the initial semantics may be lost or distorted due 
to information redistribution. It is crucial to preserve the intended semantics as much as 
possible. 
o 
Activation Function: The choice of activation function can affect the preservation of 
semantics. The CF-based activation function tends to maintain more built-in semantics 
than the sigmoid function, which can become less predictable when its slope gets steep. 
3. Knowledge Hierarchy: 
o 
Intermediate-Level Abstraction: Intermediate-level abstraction can provide advantages 
in reasoning and explanation. However, improper introduction of intermediate concepts 
can increase uncertainty and degrade system performance. 
o 
Consistent-Shift Algorithm: This algorithm is used to determine which connections in 
the hierarchy can be deleted. It helps in identifying and removing unnecessary 
intermediate concepts and rules that undermine system performance. 
4. Testing New Rules: 
o 
Acceptability of New Rules: When new rules involving intermediate or hidden concepts 
are introduced, they must be tested against instances not described by such concepts. The 
consistent-shift algorithm can be applied to determine the acceptability of these new 
rules. 
Network revision in knowledge-based neural networks is a complex but essential process for maintaining 
the accuracy and relevance of the network. It involves detecting and correcting semantically incorrect 
connections, preserving the initial semantics, and managing the knowledge hierarchy. The consistent-shift 
algorithm plays a crucial role in this process by identifying connections that need to be revised or deleted. 
The strength of the initial knowledge significantly affects the design and revision of the network, and the 
choice of activation function can influence the preservation of semantics. Proper handling of these issues 
ensures that the network remains effective and reliable over time. 
1. Effect of Initial Knowledge on Model Design: 
o 
If there is no initial knowledge, a fully connected multilayer neural network is used. 
o 
If knowledge exists, extra hidden units and connections are needed to integrate it. 
2. Uncertainty in Knowledge Completeness: 
o 
It is difficult to determine if the initial knowledge is complete. 
o 
Empirical evaluation is required, but practical constraints make this challenging. 
3. Poor Convergence Due to Hidden Units: 
o 
An inadequate number of hidden units can result in poor convergence. 
4. Knowledge Hierarchy Challenges: 
o 
Improper reasoning and incorrect abstraction levels may introduce errors. 
o 
Overfitting and performance degradation can occur due to hierarchical depth. 
5. Hidden Unit Mapping Issues:

o 
Some concepts may spread across multiple hidden units, making it difficult to retain 
semantic integrity. 
o 
Improper generalization can lead to reduced predictability. 
6. CF-Based Activation Function Limitations: 
o 
The activation function may introduce biases, affecting the adaptability of the model. 
These issues highlight the complexities of using neural networks for knowledge-based learning and 
theory revision. 
Decision Tree-Based Neural Networks 
Decision tree-based neural networks are a hybrid approach that combines the interpretability of decision 
trees with the learning capabilities of neural networks. This approach is particularly useful when the 
initial knowledge can be represented as a decision tree, which is then mapped into a neural network 
structure. 
Construction of Decision Tree-Based Neural Networks 
1. Building the Decision Tree: 
o 
Discrete Domain: For a discrete domain, the decision tree is constructed by selecting the 
best feature at each node that minimizes the entropy criterion. The entropy criterion 
measures the impurity or disorder in the data. The feature that results in the highest 
information gain (i.e., the greatest reduction in entropy) is chosen. 
o 
Continuous Domain: For a continuous domain, the decision tree is constructed by 
selecting the best hyperplane (or plane) at each node that minimizes the entropy criterion. 
This involves finding the optimal split point for continuous features. 
2. Mapping the Decision Tree to a Neural Network: 
o 
Hidden Layers: The decision tree is mapped into a neural network with two hidden 
layers. The first hidden layer corresponds to the nonleaf nodes of the decision tree, and 
the second hidden layer corresponds to the leaf nodes. 
o 
Nodes and Connections: Each nonleaf node in the decision tree becomes a node in the 
first hidden layer of the neural network. Each leaf node becomes a node in the second 
hidden layer. The connections between nodes in the neural network reflect the structure 
of the decision tree.

Constraint-Based Neural Networks 
Constraint-based neural networks are designed to solve constraint satisfaction problems, where the goal is 
to find a solution that satisfies as many given constraints as possible. These networks use semantic 
constraints to guide the learning process and ensure that the network's output adheres to the specified 
constraints. 
Types of Constraints 
1. Constraints Between Units: 
o 
These constraints are encoded as weights between units in the network. The absolute 
values of the weights reflect the strength of the constraints. A positive weight signifies a 
supporting relationship, while a negative weight indicates an incompatible relationship. 
2. Direct Constraints on Individual Units: 
o 
These constraints are implemented as external, direct inputs to individual units. The 
external input serves to clamp the unit or modify its response. For example, an external 
input can force a unit to remain active (on) or inactive (off) regardless of other inputs. 
3. Constraints for Prior Information or Probabilities: 
o 
These constraints are implemented as biases on each unit. A positive bias tends to turn a 
unit on, while a negative bias tends to shut it off. This type of constraint is useful for 
incorporating prior knowledge or probabilities into the network. 
Constraint Satisfaction Problem 
The constraint satisfaction problem involves finding a solution that maximizes the goodness of fit (G) 
value, which measures the degree to which the desired constraints are satisfied. The G value is defined as:

•

•

• 
Ij is the external input to unit j.

•

Goodness of Fit (GG): 
• 
Pairwise Constraints: The first term represents the degree to which the pairwise constraints 
between any two units are satisfied. If the weight is positive, the presence of both hypotheses 
connected by the weight will increase the G value. If the weight is negative, the presence of either 
hypothesis alone will decrease the G value. 
• 
External Input Consistency: The second term represents the consistency between the external 
input and the actual activation of each unit. The G value is increased if the external input and the 
activation level are of the same sign; otherwise, it is decreased. 
• 
Bias Influence: The third term represents the influence of the bias on the unit. If the bias and the 
actual activation are consistent in their signs, the G value is increased; otherwise, it is reduced. 
Energy Minimization 
The constraint satisfaction problem can be framed as an energy minimization problem. The energy E of 
the system is defined as the negative of the G value: 
E=−G 
The goal is to minimize the energy E, which corresponds to maximizing the G value. The Hopfield 
network, a type of recurrent neural network, can be used to solve this problem. The network iteratively 
updates the states of its units to find a stable state that minimizes the energy. 
Asynchronous Update Rule: 
• 
To avoid the problem of units inhibiting each other simultaneously, an asynchronous update rule 
is used. This rule ensures that only one unit updates its state at a time, allowing the network to 
explore different states and converge to a solution that satisfies the constraints. 
Summary 
• 
Decision Tree-Based Neural Networks: These networks combine the interpretability of decision 
trees with the learning capabilities of neural networks. The decision tree is mapped into a neural 
network with two hidden layers, and the network is trained using standard algorithms like 
backpropagation. 
• 
Constraint-Based Neural Networks: These networks solve constraint satisfaction problems by 
incorporating semantic constraints into the network's structure. The constraints are encoded as 
weights, external inputs, and biases. The goal is to maximize the goodness of fit (G) value, which 
measures the degree to which the constraints are satisfied. The problem can be framed as an 
energy minimization problem, and techniques like the Hopfield network and asynchronous update 
rules are used to find optimal solutions.

UNIT IV
Optimization for Training Deep 
Models

Introduction
•
In deep learning, an optimizer is a crucial element that dynamically fine-
tune a model’s parameters throughout the training process, aiming to
minimize a predefined loss function. Its primary role is to minimize the
model’s
error
or
loss
function,
enhancing
performance.
Various
optimization algorithms, known as optimizers, employ distinct strategies
to converge towards optimal parameter values for improved predictions
efficiently.
•
These specialized algorithms facilitate the learning process of neural
networks by iteratively refining the weights and biases based on the
feedback received from the data.
•
Each optimizer is equipped with distinct update rules, learning rates, and
momentum strategies, all geared towards the overarching goal of
discovering and converging upon optimal model parameters, thereby
enhancing overall performance.
•
Stochastic Gradient Descent, Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, Adagrad,
RMSProp, AdaDelta, and Adam

Important Deep Learning Terms
Before proceeding, there are a few terms that you should be 
familiar with.
• Epoch – The number of times the algorithm runs on the 
whole training dataset.
• Sample – A single row of a dataset.
• Batch – It denotes the number of samples to be taken to 
for updating the model parameters.
• Learning rate – It is a parameter that provides the model a 
scale of how much model weights should be updated.
• Cost Function/Loss Function – A cost function is used to 
calculate the cost, which is the difference between the 
predicted value and the actual value.
• Weights/ Bias – The learnable parameters in a model that 
controls the signal between two neurons.

How Learning Differs from Pure 
Optimization
• learning is not just about optimizing a cost function. 
Instead, learning in deep models has additional 
challenges beyond pure optimization.
• Generalization vs. Optimization
• In traditional optimization, the goal is to find the 
lowest possible value of the objective function.
• In machine learning, particularly deep learning, the 
main goal is generalization—ensuring the model 
performs well on unseen data.
• A model that overfits training data may achieve low 
cost but fail to generalize. Hence, the best optimization 
result is not always the best learning outcome.

Ill-Conditioning of Cost Functions
•
Deep learning cost functions can have flat regions, sharp ridges, or
chaotic landscapes, making pure optimization inefficient.
•
Algorithms like Adam and RMSprop help navigate these difficult
optimization surfaces.
Role of Regularization
•
Regularization
techniques
(L1/L2
penalties,
dropout,
data
augmentation) modify the optimization process to encourage
better generalization.
•
This differs from pure optimization, which only seeks to minimize
the cost function without considering overfitting.
Optimization Does Not Necessarily Need to Reach Global Minimum
•
Unlike convex optimization problems where the global minimum is
ideal, deep learning models often work well with local minima or
even saddle points.
•
Empirical studies show that many local minima in deep networks
have similar generalization performance.

Noisy and Stochastic Training
•
Unlike
deterministic
optimization
problems,
deep
learning
involves
stochasticity due to random weight initialization, mini-batch training, and
data noise.
•
Methods like SGD leverage this stochastic nature to help escape saddle
points and improve generalization.
Implicit Bias of Optimization Algorithms
•
Different optimization algorithms (SGD, Adam, etc.) introduce biases that
affect model performance.
•
SGD, for example, tends to favor solutions with better generalization
properties, even if they are not the absolute minima.

Challenges in Optimization for 
Training Deep Models
Optimizing deep neural networks is much more complex than optimizing simple 
functions. Several challenges arise due to the high-dimensional, non-convex nature 
of deep learning cost functions. Below are some of the key challenges in 
optimization:
1. Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
•
During backpropagation, gradients can become extremely small (vanishing) or 
excessively large (exploding), making training unstable.
•
This typically occurs in deep networks where repeated multiplication of small or 
large derivatives leads to extreme values.
–
Vanishing gradients slow down learning, especially in earlier layers.
–
Exploding gradients cause weight updates to be too large, leading to instability.
To overcome:
–
Use activation functions like ReLU instead of sigmoid or tanh.
–
Employ batch normalization to normalize activations.
–
Use gradient clipping to prevent extreme values.

Poor Conditioning of the Cost Function
•
The optimization landscape may contain regions where 
gradients change rapidly in some directions and slowly in 
others.
•
Happens when the Hessian matrix (second derivative of 
the cost function) has a high condition number, leading to 
slow convergence.
– Standard gradient descent struggles with poorly conditioned 
surfaces.
– Training can take much longer to converge.
• To overcome
– Use adaptive learning rate algorithms like RMSprop, Adam, or 
Adagrad.
– Apply batch normalization to improve conditioning.
– Scale input features properly to ensure a well-behaved cost 
function.

Saddle Points and Local Minima
•
Unlike convex optimization, where there is one global 
minimum, deep learning cost functions contain many local 
minima and saddle points (where the gradient is zero but it 
is neither a minimum nor a maximum).
•
High-dimensional spaces often have many saddle points, 
making optimization harder.
– SGD and other optimizers can get stuck in these regions, slowing 
down training.
– Many local minima may perform equally well, but poor local 
minima can degrade generalization.
• To overcome
– Use stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with momentum to help 
escape saddle points.
– Adaptive optimization methods like Adam can help navigate 
complex landscapes.
– Introduce random weight initialization to prevent poor local 
minima trapping.

Choosing the Right Learning Rate
•
A learning rate that is too high causes divergence, while a 
rate that is too low results in slow convergence.
– Poorly chosen learning rates lead to inefficient training and may 
cause oscillations.
To overcome
– Use learning rate schedules (e.g., step decay, cosine annealing, 
or cyclical learning rates).
– Implement adaptive learning rate algorithms (Adam, RMSprop, 
Adagrad).
– Perform hyperparameter tuning to find an optimal learning 
rate.

Computational Cost and Hardware Limitations
• Training deep models requires substantial computational 
resources, making optimization time-consuming.
– Large-scale datasets and deep models demand high GPU/TPU 
memory.
– Optimization algorithms can be inefficient when dealing with large-
scale deep networks.
• To overcome:
– Use mini-batch training instead of full-batch updates.
– Optimize computation using parallel processing and distributed 
training.
– Use model pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation to 
reduce computational overhead.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity
•
Deep learning models depend heavily on hyperparameters (e.g., learning 
rate, batch size, momentum). Small changes can drastically impact 
performance.
– Poorly chosen hyperparameters lead to slow convergence or instability.
•
To overcome
– Use automated hyperparameter tuning (grid search, random search, Bayesian 
optimization).
– Experiment with different batch sizes and optimizers to find an optimal 
balance.
Optimizing deep neural networks involves more than just minimizing a function—it
requires navigating challenges like vanishing gradients, saddle points, generalization,
and computational constraints. Modern deep learning techniques employ various
adaptive learning rates, regularization methods, and specialized optimization
algorithms to address these challenges effectively.

Basic Algorithms
Stochastic Gradient Descent(SGD)
SGD is one of the most widely used algorithms for training deep learning models.
•
Gradient Descent involves computing the gradient of the cost function with respect to the
parameters across the entire training set.
•
Stochastic Gradient Descent accelerates this by computing the gradient based on a randomly
selected mini-batch of examples. This provides a noisy but efficient estimate of the true
gradient.

Momentum
•
While stochastic gradient descent remains a very popular optimization strategy, learning with it can 
sometimes be slow. The method of momentum (Polyak 1964 , ) is designed to accelerate learning, 
especially in the face of high curvature, small but consistent gradients, or noisy gradients. The momentum 
algorithm accumulates an exponentially decaying moving average of past gradients and continues to move 
in their direction. 
•
Momentum improves SGD by helping the optimizer build velocity in directions of consistent gradient 
descent, reducing oscillations.
•
Mechanism:
•
Instead of updating the parameters purely by the current gradient, momentum introduces a velocity 
vector that aggregates past gradients.
•
This technique helps traverse ravines(deep narrow steeps) and escape small local minima more effectively.

Parameter Initialization Strategies
When you train a neural network, we need to assig initial values to the weights (and sometimes 
biases). This process is called parameter initialization.
When training deep neural networks, how you initialize the weights can have a huge impact on:
•
Convergence speed
•
Gradient flow (avoiding vanishing/exploding gradients)
•
The quality of the final solution
Improper initialization may:
•
Cause the network to converge very slowly
•
Lead to dead neurons (especially with ReLU activations)
•
Make gradients either explode or vanish, especially in deep networks
•
Get stuck (bad local minimum)
•
Diverge (exploding gradients)
•
Learn slowly or not at all
A good initialization:
•
Breaks symmetry between neurons (each neuron should learn different things)
•
Avoids vanishing gradients (very small gradients, causing no learning)
•
Avoids exploding gradients (very large gradients, causing instability)
•
Speeds up learning
•
Sets up the model to generalize better

Basic Techniques
1. Random Initialization
•
Weights are randomly sampled from a uniform or normal distribution.
•
The scale (spread) of this randomness is very important.
–
Too small → weak signals, vanishing gradients
–
Too large → exploding activations or gradients
2. Symmetry Breaking
•
If all neurons in a layer start with the same weights, they learn the same features.
•
Random initialization ensures each neuron follows a different trajectory during training.
3. Scaling the Initialization
•
To maintain signal flow across layers, the weights are often scaled based on:
•
Number of inputs (fan-in)
•
Number of outputs (fan-out)

Orthogonal Initialization
•
Weights are initialized as orthogonal matrices (like perpendicular vectors).
•
Keeps signal stable across layers (used especially in RNNs).
Sparse Initialization
•
Only a few weights per neuron are non-zero.
•
Helps large networks avoid overfitting early on.
Bias Initialization
•
Usually set to 0.
•
Sometimes a small positive constant (e.g., 0.1 for ReLU) to prevent units from "dying".
•
For output layers: set biases to match the expected distribution (e.g., logit of class probabilities).
Learning-Based Initialization
Instead of random values, sometimes we initialize using:
•
Pretrained models (e.g., pretraining on ImageNet)
•
Unsupervised pretraining (like autoencoders)
•
Transfer learning (weights from one task reused in another)
Problems Addressed by Good Initialization
•
Vanishing gradients: When gradients shrink as they propagate backward, halting learning.
•
Exploding gradients: When gradients grow exponentially, destabilizing learning.
•
Proper scaling of weights prevents both problems by maintaining the variance of the forward 
activations and backward gradients across layers.

Algorithms with Adaptive Learning Rates
Setting the right learning rate is critical in training deep networks. A too-small
learning rate leads to slow learning; a too-large one causes the training to diverge.
The idea behind adaptive learning rate methods is:
•
Use different learning rates for different parameters.
•
Automatically adjust those learning rates during training.
Early Solution: Delta-Bar-Delta Algorithm
Introduced by Jacobs (1988), it was one of the first attempts to adapt the learning 
rate per parameter.
main Idea:
•
If a parameter’s gradient keeps the same sign (e.g., always negative), it means 
we’re on a consistent slope → increase learning rate.
•
If the gradient changes sign (e.g., from negative to positive), it might mean we 
overshot the minimum → decrease learning rate.
Limitation:
•
It works well only with full-batch training (i.e., using the entire dataset at once), 
which is not practical for modern large-scale deep learning.

Modern Adaptive Methods
As training shifted to mini-batches (small batches of data), newer algorithms 
were needed to:
•
Adapt learning rates for each parameter
•
Work with mini-batch gradients
•
Handle noisy gradient estimates efficiently
This leads to modern adaptive optimizers like:
•
AdaGrad
•
RMSProp
•
Adam
These optimizers learn how to adjust the learning rate automatically for each
parameter during training.

AdaGrad
AdaGrad stands for Adaptive Gradient Algorithm.
It’s an optimization algorithm that adapts the learning rate for each parameter individually 
during training.
Instead of using a single learning rate for all weights, AdaGrad:
Scales down the learning rate proportionally to the historical sum of squared gradients
for each parameter.
This means: parameters that learn quickly (large gradients) will slow down over time.
And parameters that learn slowly (small gradients) will retain higher learning rates.
So:
Big gradients → slower updates
Small gradients → faster updates
This helps the optimizer to:
•Take larger steps in flatter directions of the loss surface.
•Take smaller steps in steep directions.

RMSProp
RMSProp (Root Mean Square Propagation) is an adaptive learning rate optimization
algorithm - just like AdaGrad — but it fixes one major problem with AdaGrad, i.e. It
doesn’t let the learning rate decay too much.
Problem with AdaGrad:
•
AdaGrad accumulates all past squared gradients.
•
Over time, this makes the denominator in its update rule grow very large, causing 
the effective learning rate to shrink toward zero.
Sol: Instead of accumulating the entire history, RMSProp uses an exponentially 
decaying average of the squared gradients.
RMSProp (Root Mean Square Propagation) is an adaptive learning rate algorithm that:
•
Adjusts the learning rate individually for each parameter.
•
Uses a moving average of squared gradients to prevent the learning rate from 
shrinking too much (a problem in AdaGrad).

Adam Optimizer
Adam stands for Adaptive Moment Estimation.
It is one of the most widely used optimizers in deep learning today.
It is a combination of:
•
Momentum (tracks past gradients to smooth updates)
•
RMSProp (adapts learning rates based on recent squared gradients)
Adam combines both stability and adaptiveness.
1. Tracks first moment (mean of gradients) → like momentum
•
Helps keep a consistent update direction
2. Tracks second moment (variance of gradients) → like RMSProp
•
Helps scale learning rate properly for each parameter
3. Bias Correction
•
Since both moment estimates start at zero, Adam includes 
correction terms early in training to prevent bias in those 
estimates.

Choosing the Right Optimizer: Which One Is Best?
•
Deep learning problems are diverse, and different tasks respond better to 
different optimizers.
•
There's no single algorithm that consistently outperforms all others across all 
tasks.

ABSTRACT  
  
  
Shelf life prediction of leafy vegetables is essential to ensure food safety, maintain nutritional quality, 
and reduce post-harvest losses. Leafy vegetables such as spinach are highly perishable due to their high 
moisture content and are prone to rapid deterioration caused by wilting, yellowing, texture changes, and 
microbial growth. Traditional methods of assessing freshness rely on manual inspection or laboratory 
testing, which are time-consuming, subjective, and often inefficient.  
  
This project proposes an AI-based shelf life prediction system that uses image analysis to 
evaluate the freshness of leafy vegetables and estimate their remaining shelf life. The system analyzes 
visual features such as color variation, texture, and structural changes to classify the produce into 
different freshness stages - Fresh, Mid-life, and Near Spoilage. Based on this classification, the model 
estimates the remaining shelf life in days, providing a fast, non-destructive, and automated solution.  
  
By integrating image preprocessing and machine learning techniques, the proposed system aims 
to support better storage decisions, reduce food wastage, and promote sustainable food management 
practices. Spinach is used as a prototype to develop and validate the model, demonstrating the practical 
applicability of AI in improving post-harvest quality  assessment.

1. INTRODUCTION  
  
1.1 Motivation  
  
  
Leafy vegetables are an essential part of a healthy diet, providing vital nutrients, vitamins, and minerals. 
However, they are also among the most perishable food products due to their high moisture content and 
delicate structure. Vegetables such as spinach deteriorate rapidly after harvest, leading to wilting, 
discoloration, texture degradation, and microbial spoilage. This short shelf life creates major challenges 
in storage, transportation, and retail management.  
  
In many cases, freshness is assessed through manual inspection, which is subjective and inconsistent. 
Laboratory testing methods, although accurate, are time-consuming and not feasible for everyday use 
by farmers, vendors, or consumers. As a result, produce is often discarded prematurely or consumed 
when quality has already declined. This not only leads to economic losses but also contributes 
significantly to food wastage and environmental impact.  
  
With the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence and image processing technologies, there is an 
opportunity to develop an automated, non-destructive, and efficient system for freshness evaluation. The 
motivation behind this project is to create an AI-based shelf life prediction system that can analyze visual 
features of leafy vegetables and provide reliable freshness classification and remaining shelf life 
estimation. By offering a smart and practical solution, this project aims to reduce post-harvest losses, 
support better decision-making, and promote sustainable food management practices.  
1.2 Existing Systems  
  
  
Currently, shelf life prediction of leafy vegetables is primarily carried out using traditional and manual 
methods. One of the most common approaches is manual inspection, where freshness is judged based 
on visible characteristics such as leaf color, texture, firmness, and presence of wilting. However, this 
method is highly subjective, varies from person to person, and is not reliable for large-scale evaluation.  
  
Another widely used approach is laboratory and chemical testing, which involves microbial analysis 
and chemical degradation studies. While these methods provide accurate results, they are time-
consuming, expensive, and unsuitable for real-time or on-field assessment. They require specialized 
equipment and trained personnel, making them impractical for farmers, vendors, and retailers.

Sensor-based techniques are also used in some cases, where temperature and humidity levels are 
monitored to indirectly estimate shelf life. Although useful, these systems require additional hardware 
infrastructure and do not directly analyze the visual quality of the vegetables.  
  
Traditional computer vision methods with basic machine learning techniques have also been explored. 
These methods rely on handcrafted features such as color thresholding and texture extraction. However, 
they lack robustness and often show lower accuracy compared to modern deep learning approaches.  
  
Overall, existing systems are either subjective, expensive, indirect, or limited in accuracy, highlighting 
the need for an automated, non-destructive, and AI-based solution for effective shelf life prediction.  
1.3 Literature Survey  
Several research studies and technological advancements highlight the importance of using AI and 
image processing techniques for predicting the quality and shelf life of perishable produce:  
  
  
Many researchers have explored computer vision methods to evaluate the freshness of vegetables and 
fruits by analyzing visual features like color, texture, and shape. Traditional machine learning models 
such as SVM, k-NN, and decision trees have been used to classify freshness levels based on handcrafted 
features extracted from images. Although these methods showed promising results, their performance 
was limited by the quality of feature extraction and sensitivity to lighting variations.  
  
  
Recent studies show improved results with deep learning models, especially Convolutional Neural 
Networks (CNNs), which can automatically learn important visual features without manual intervention. 
CNN-based approaches have been used widely in food quality assessment, including prediction of 
ripeness, spoilage, and defect detection in fruits and vegetables. These models demonstrated higher 
accuracy and robustness compared to classical image processing techniques.  
  
  
Research has also been conducted on shelf life estimation using both physical sensor data and visual 
analysis. For example, multispectral imaging and hyperspectral analysis have been used to monitor 
biochemical changes in produce, enabling more accurate shelf life prediction. However, these systems 
often require specialized and expensive equipment, limiting their practical usability.

Studies focusing on AI-based non-destructive methods highlight the potential of combining image 
analysis with machine learning to predict remaining shelf life in real time. These approaches are 
advantageous because they are faster, more cost-effective, and can be integrated with mobile or 
embedded systems for on-field use.  
Overall, literature emphasizes that AI-based image analysis, particularly deep learning techniques, offers 
significant improvements in freshness classification and shelf life  
prediction compared to traditional methods, motivating further development in this area.  
  
  
  
1.4 Challenges to existing system  
  
The existing methods for shelf life prediction of leafy vegetables face several limitations. Manual 
inspection, which is widely used, is highly subjective and depends on individual judgment. Different 
people may assess freshness differently, leading to inconsistent and unreliable results. This method is 
also not scalable for large quantities in markets or storage facilities.  
  
  
Laboratory and chemical testing methods, although accurate, are time-consuming, expensive, and 
require specialized equipment and trained personnel. These techniques are not suitable for real-time 
evaluation or regular monitoring in farms, retail shops, or supply chains.  
  
  
Sensor-based approaches that monitor environmental factors such as temperature and humidity provide 
only indirect estimation of freshness. They do not analyze the actual visual or structural condition of the 
leafy vegetables and require additional hardware infrastructure, increasing cost and complexity.  
  
  
Traditional computer vision techniques using basic machine learning rely on handcrafted features like 
color thresholding and texture extraction. These methods often struggle with variations in lighting, 
background noise, and image quality, resulting in lower accuracy and poor generalization.  
  
  
Overall, the key challenges in existing systems include subjectivity, high cost, lack of real-time 
capability, dependency on external hardware, and limited prediction accuracy. These limitations 
highlight the need for an automated, robust, and AI-based non-destructive solution for effective shelf 
life prediction.

1.5 Proposed System  
The proposed system is an AI-based shelf life prediction model for leafy vegetables that uses image 
analysis to classify freshness stages and estimate the remaining shelf life. The system captures RGB 
images of leafy vegetables such as spinach, mint, coriander, and cabbage using a camera. These images 
are preprocessed through resizing, normalization, and augmentation to ensure consistent input quality.  
  
  
A deep learning approach using Transfer Learning with MobileNetV2 is implemented to automatically 
extract important visual features such as color degradation, texture variation, and wilting patterns. The 
model classifies the vegetable into three freshness categories: Fresh, Mild (Mid-life), and Rotten (Near 
Spoilage). Based on the predicted category, the system estimates the remaining shelf life in days using 
a classification-to-time mapping approach.  
  
  
Unlike traditional methods, the proposed system provides a fast, automated, and non- destructive 
evaluation of freshness without requiring laboratory testing or additional sensor infrastructure. It reduces 
human error, improves prediction accuracy, and enables real-time freshness assessment. This system 
aims to minimize post-harvest losses, support better storage and supply chain decisions, and promote 
sustainable food management practices.

1.7 Methodology  
  
The methodology of the proposed shelf life prediction system consists of several structured steps, 
starting from data collection to final prediction.  
  
  
Initially, a dataset of leafy vegetable images (such as spinach, mint, coriander, and cabbage) was 
collected and categorized into three freshness classes: Fresh, Mild (Mid- life), and Rotten. The dataset 
was then divided into training, validation, and testing sets to ensure proper model evaluation.  
  
  
In the preprocessing stage, all images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels to match the input requirements 
of the model. Normalization was applied to scale pixel values, and data augmentation techniques such 
as rotation, flipping, and zooming were used to improve model generalization and reduce overfitting.  
For model development, Transfer Learning was applied using a pre-trained MobileNetV2 model. The 
base model (trained on ImageNet) was frozen to retain learned features, and additional layers such as 
Global Average Pooling, Dropout (0.5), and a Dense output layer with Softmax activation were added 
for multi-class classification.  
The model was trained using the Adam optimizer and categorical cross-entropy loss function. Early 
stopping was implemented to prevent overfitting and improve training efficiency.

percentage. Based on the predicted category, the system estimates the remaining shelf life in days using 
a predefined classification-to-time mapping approach.

2. PROPOSED SYSTEM  
  
2.1 Architecture  
  
The architecture of the proposed Shelf Life Prediction system is based on a deep learning model using 
Transfer Learning with the MobileNetV2 convolutional neural network. The system processes input 
images of leafy vegetables and classifies them into different freshness stages.  
  
  
Initially, the system accepts an input image of size 224 × 224 × 3, which represents an RGB image of 
the leafy vegetable. The image is then passed to the MobileNetV2 model, which is pre-trained on the 
ImageNet dataset. In this architecture, the base layers of MobileNetV2 are kept frozen so that the 
previously learned features such as edges, textures, and color patterns can be effectively utilized for 
feature extraction.  
The extracted feature maps are then passed through a Global Average Pooling 2D layer, which converts 
the high-dimensional feature maps into a one-dimensional feature vector. This helps reduce the number 
of parameters and simplifies the model while preserving important information.  
  
  
Next, a Dropout layer with a dropout rate of 0.5 is applied. This layer randomly deactivates some 
neurons during training, which helps in reducing overfitting and improves the generalization capability 
of the model.  
  
  
The processed features are then passed to a Dense layer consisting of three neurons. A Softmax 
activation function is used in this layer to generate probability values for each class.

8  
Finally, the system classifies the input image into one of the three freshness categories: Fresh, Mild, or 
Rotten. Along with the predicted class, the system also provides a confidence score, indicating the 
probability of the prediction. This architecture enables efficient feature extraction, accurate 
classification, and reliable freshness stage detection for leafy vegetables.  
 
  
2.2 Module level design  
The Shelf  Life Prediction system is divided into several functional modules that work together to 
classify the freshness stage of leafy vegetables and estimate their remaining shelf life.  
  
  
1. Image Input Module  
  
This module is responsible for acquiring the input image of the leafy vegetable. The image is captured 
using a camera or selected from a dataset. The input image is resized to 224 × 224 × 3 to match the input 
requirements of the deep learning model.  
  
  
2. Feature Extraction Module  
  
In this module, the input image is passed to the MobileNetV2 model, which is pre-trained on the 
ImageNet dataset. The base layers of the model are kept frozen so that previously learned features such 
as edges, color patterns, and textures can be effectively used to extract meaningful information from the 
image.

4. Regularization Module  
  
A Dropout layer with a rate of 0.5 is applied to the feature vector to reduce overfitting. This module

3. IMPLEMENTATION and TESTING  
  
3.1 Implementation  
The implementation of the Shelf Life Prediction system was carried out in a systematic manner, covering 
dataset preparation, preprocessing, model development, training, and prediction. The system was 
developed using Python along with deep learning frameworks such as TensorFlow/Keras.  
  
  
3.1.1 Dataset Preparation  
  
  
  
Images of selected leafy vegetables such as spinach, mint, coriander, and cabbage were collected and 
categorized into three freshness classes: Fresh, Mild (Mid-life), and Rotten. The dataset was organized 
into separate folders based on these categories. The complete dataset was divided into training and 
validation sets to enable effective model learning and performance monitoring.  
  
  
3.1.2 Data Preprocessing  
  
  
  
All images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels to match the input requirements of the MobileNetV2 model. 
Pixel values were normalized to improve training efficiency and convergence. Data augmentation 
techniques such as rotation, horizontal flipping, and zooming were applied to increase dataset diversity 
and enhance the robustness of the model.  
  
  
3.1.3 Model Development  
  
  
  
Transfer Learning was implemented using the pre-trained MobileNetV2 model with ImageNet weights. 
The base layers were frozen to preserve previously learned features. Additional layers were added, 
including a Global Average Pooling layer to reduce feature dimensions, a Dropout layer (0.5) to 
minimize overfitting, and a Dense output layer with Softmax activation consisting of three neurons 
representing Fresh, Mild, and Rotten categories.

11  
3.1.4 Model Training  
  
  
  
The model was compiled using the Adam optimizer and categorical cross-entropy loss function. Training 
was performed over multiple epochs while monitoring validation performance. Early stopping was 
applied to prevent overfitting and ensure optimal model performance.  
  
  
3.1.5 Prediction and Shelf Life Estimation  
  
  
  
After training, the model was used to classify new input images into one of the three freshness categories. 
The Softmax layer generated probability scores along with a confidence percentage. Based on the 
predicted freshness class, a classification-to-time mapping approach was applied to estimate the 
remaining shelf life in days, providing the final output of the system.  
  
  
  
  
  
3.2 Testing  
  
The testing phase was conducted to evaluate the performance and reliability of the proposed Shelf Life 
Prediction system. After training the model, it was tested using unseen images from the test dataset to 
assess its generalization capability.  
  
  
During testing, input images were passed through the trained MobileNetV2-based model, and the 
predicted freshness category (Fresh, Mild, or Rotten) along with the confidence percentage was 
recorded. The predicted results were compared with the actual labels to measure classification accuracy.  
  
  
Performance evaluation was carried out using accuracy as the primary metric. The model demonstrated 
satisfactory accuracy in classifying freshness stages of leafy vegetables, particularly spinach used as the 
prototype.

1.1 Motivation 
Undergoing surgery is usually one of the scariest things a human being can go 
through — not merely physically, but emotionally, intellectually, and financially too. It 
is an experience of uncertainty, fear, and life-and-death choices, but most patients are 
left with next to no information about how to handle the ordeal. Numerous individuals 
feel suffocated by basic questions which should have very simple answers: Which 
hospital or physician can I trust with my life? How much is going to cost this procedure 
and if so, whether I am able to pay for it? Do I qualify for any government plans, 
insurance programs, or payment plans to assist me? These are not trivial fears — they're 
profoundly human anxieties that influence whether, when, or even if someone chooses 
to have life-saving or life-enhancing surgery. The healthcare system, too often, doesn't 
make it convenient to learn these things. Data is scattered across various channels, 
medical terminology can be confusing, and assistance seems out of reach or 
nonexistent. 
That's what drove us to design SurgiAssist — an intuitive, intelligent, and 
effective tool designed with compassion and fueled by the conviction that each patient 
should have transparency, access, and respect in their healthcare experience.

find and compare hospitals in terms of quality, distance, and patient review. It refers 
them to veteran, reputable surgeons and specialists most appropriate for them. It 
expatiates procedure prices in ways easy to grasp, and — above all, probably — exposes

At its heart, SurgiAssist is about something more profound than logistics or

taking fright and making sense of it. It's about turning confusion into understanding. It's 
about allowing patients to be heard, to be understood, and to be in control, to make 
informed decisions on their own behalf, and sometimes the behalf of their loved ones.

1.7 Methodology 
The creation of SurgiAssist was a systematic and user-oriented process, aiming 
to make surgical healthcare data readable and easily understandable to individuals from 
all walks of society. Right from the beginning, the aim was to integrate surgery, 
availability of hospitals, costs, and health scheme eligibility under one single, easy-to-
use platform. A simple, responsive frontend was created with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, 
and Flask's Jinja2 template engine. It had an easy-to-use interface with a categorized 
list of surgical procedures and well-defined navigation paths, enabling users to easily 
transition from general surgery listings to detailed hospital and procedure pages. With 
responsiveness guaranteed across devices, the interface was made to be both visually 
pleasing and functionally efficient for varied user needs. 
 
After the frontend was set up, backend integration started, driven by a MySQL 
database that was capable of dynamically loading and structuring data regarding 
hospitals, procedures, expenses, and government schemes. SQL JOIN queries enabled 
the fetching of related data in one request, providing users with immediate access to 
detailed procedure and hospital data. Flask managed the server-side functionality, 
translating user input into backend procedures and presenting the result through Jinja2 
templates for uniformity and ease of scalability. With time, the system integrated 
functional features such as health scheme eligibility tags, web links to hospitals, and 
integrated Google Maps for easier navigation. The changes involved in the database 
schema and interface designs, but were gracefully implemented to make the system 
more usable without intimidating the user. 
For system resilience, rigorous local testing occurred at all development phases. 
End-to-end tests, such as user authentication, data validation, and edge cases, 
guaranteed that the platform provided a consistent experience across features. Local

Database Integration 
SurgiAssist is tightly integrated with a MySQL database that serves as the central 
repository for all application data. The system follows a relational model, consisting of 
multiple interrelated tables. These include tables for surgeries, hospitals, procedure 
offerings, insurance schemes, coverage information, and user credentials. 
The structure is designed to be normalized, reducing data redundancy and ensuring 
consistency. Relationships between entities such as surgeries and hospitals are managed 
using foreign keys and join tables. For example, the linkage between procedures and 
hospitals is handled through a mapping table that also stores cost information, while 
scheme coverage is represented through a separate table that connects procedures to 
government or private schemes. 
The application logic is written to handle real-time queries that retrieve and process 
data based on user inputs, such as cost range filters or scheme availability. Efficient

logic to generate tailored views for users.

ABSTRACT  
  
  
Shelf life prediction of leafy vegetables is essential to ensure food safety, maintain nutritional 
quality, and reduce post-harvest losses. Leafy vegetables such as spinach are highly perishable 
due to their high moisture content and are prone to rapid deterioration caused by wilting, 
yellowing, texture changes, and microbial growth. Traditional methods of assessing freshness 
rely on manual inspection or laboratory testing, which are time-consuming, subjective, and 
often inefficient.  
  
This project proposes an AI-based shelf life prediction system that uses image analysis 
to evaluate the freshness of leafy vegetables and estimate their remaining shelf life. The system 
analyzes visual features such as color variation, texture, and structural changes to classify the 
produce into different freshness stages - Fresh, Mid-life, and Near Spoilage. Based on this 
classification, the model estimates the remaining shelf life in days, providing a fast, non-
destructive, and automated solution.  
  
By integrating image preprocessing and machine learning techniques, the proposed 
system aims to support better storage decisions, reduce food wastage, and promote sustainable 
food management practices. Spinach is used as a prototype to develop and validate the model, 
demonstrating the practical applicability of AI in improving post-harvest quality 
 assessment.
